title: NASM Macros and Conditional Assembly
summary: Writing less assembly by hand - single-line macros with %define, multi-line macros with %macro and their parameters, local labels with %%, repeating code with %rep and %assign, choosing code with %if and %ifdef, and macros that generate whole functions.
markdown:
## The preprocessor

Before NASM assembles anything, its **preprocessor** expands macros, much as C's preprocessor does (C course lesson 5.04). Macros remove repetition that functions cannot: saving the same registers in every function, unrolling a loop, defining a family of similar functions.

## %define: single-line macros

```nasm-norun
%define SYS_WRITE   1
%define SYS_EXIT    60
%define STDOUT      1
%define ELEMENT(base, i)  [base + (i) * 8]     ; a macro with parameters

        mov     eax, SYS_WRITE
        mov     rax, ELEMENT(rdi, 3)          ; becomes mov rax, [rdi + (3) * 8]
```

`%define` is pure text replacement. `equ` (lesson 1.05) defines a number the assembler knows; `%define` can stand for any text, including registers and operands.

## %macro: multi-line macros

A multi-line macro has a name and a **number of parameters**; inside, `%1`, `%2` ... are the arguments:

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .text

%macro EXIT 1
        mov     eax, 60
        mov     edi, %1
        syscall
%endmacro

%macro PRINT_NUMBER 1
        mov     rdi, %1
        call    print_int
        call    print_newline
%endmacro

_start:
        mov     rbx, 6
        imul    rbx, 7
        PRINT_NUMBER rbx            ; 42
        PRINT_NUMBER 100
        EXIT    0
```

A range like `%macro SAVE 1-3` accepts one to three arguments; `%0` is how many were given.

## Local labels: %%

A label inside a macro would be defined twice if the macro is used twice. Prefixing it with `%%` makes NASM invent a fresh name at each use:

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .text

; CLAMP reg, low, high: keeps reg between low and high (registers or numbers).
%macro CLAMP 3
        cmp     %1, %2
        jge     %%not_low
        mov     %1, %2
%%not_low:
        cmp     %1, %3
        jle     %%done
        mov     %1, %3
%%done:
%endmacro

_start:
        mov     rax, -40
        CLAMP   rax, 0, 255
        mov     rdi, rax
        call    print_int               ; 0
        call    print_newline
        mov     rax, 900
        CLAMP   rax, 0, 255
        mov     rdi, rax
        call    print_int               ; 255
        call    print_newline
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

## Repeating: %rep and %assign

`%rep n ... %endrep` copies its body n times. `%assign` sets a number the preprocessor can compute with, so each copy can be different. Together they **unroll** a loop:

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .data
numbers: dq     3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6
        section .text

; sum8: rdi = an array of exactly 8 qwords. No loop counter, no jumps.
sum8:
        xor     eax, eax
%assign i 0
%rep 8
        add     rax, [rdi + i * 8]
%assign i i + 1
%endrep
        ret

_start:
        lea     rdi, [rel numbers]
        call    sum8
        mov     rdi, rax
        call    print_int               ; 31
        call    print_newline
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

The listing of the assembled program shows eight `add` instructions with offsets 0, 8, 16 ... 56.

## Choosing code: %if and %ifdef

```nasm-norun
%define DEBUG 1

%if DEBUG
        call    dump_registers          ; only assembled when DEBUG is non-zero
%endif

%ifdef WINDOWS
        ; the Windows calling convention
%else
        ; System V
%endif
```

Pass definitions on the command line with `nasm -dDEBUG=1 ...` to build different versions from one source.

## Macros that write functions

A macro can produce a whole function, with names glued together from its parameters:

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .text

%macro MAKE_SCALER 2                    ; name, factor
scale_%1:
        mov     rax, rdi
        imul    rax, %2
        ret
%endmacro

MAKE_SCALER double, 2
MAKE_SCALER triple, 3
MAKE_SCALER dozen, 12

_start:
        mov     edi, 5
        call    scale_dozen
        mov     rdi, rax
        call    print_int               ; 60
        call    print_newline
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

## When to use them

Macros are great for boilerplate that must be identical everywhere (prologues, system calls, error checks) and for unrolling. Overused, they hide what the code really does and make debugging harder, because the debugger shows the expanded instructions. A plain `call` to a function is often clearer and smaller.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? Why does a label in a macro need `%%`?
+ Without it, using the macro twice would define the same label twice
- `%%` makes the label global so other files can jump to it
- Labels inside macros are not allowed without a prefix
> `%%loop` gets a new unique name every time the macro is expanded, so two uses do not clash.

? What is the difference between `%rep` and a loop?
- `%rep` runs faster because it uses a hidden counter register
+ `%rep` copies the code when assembling
- `%rep` repeats the code only in debug builds
> After `%rep 4` the code appears four times in the output, with no counter or jump. A loop is assembled once and runs several times.

? Inside %macro ADD3 3, what is %2?
- the macro's name
+ the second argument of the use
- the number of arguments
- a local label
> %1, %2 and %3 are the arguments; %0 is how many were given.
```
